title: Lena and the Smile
premise: Folklorist Lena Nakamura returns to his grandmother's decaying house in the mountain village of Kessho to record its dying songs, but every photograph taken there now shows an extra chair at the table — a chair that appears closer each day. The village's oldest resident, Auntie Sato, is preparing to sign the house over to a development company, and local legend says when the last name is signed, whatever has been waiting will finally sit down. As Lena's family is drawn back one by one by letters they never sent, he realizes the chair counts down to a claiming that began with his grandfather's broken promise. In the end, Lena chooses truth over loyalty: he publicly sings the forbidden song, names what his family did, and offers himself as the resident who signs — not surrendering, but renegotiating the debt, leaving the house standing and empty, the chair finally occupied by nothing but memory.
about_author: Lior Winterbourne is the pen name of a former archivist of regional oral traditions who spent a decade transcribing songs in remote mountain communities before turning to fiction. They write horror rooted in folklore, inheritance, and the quiet violence of things families refuse to say aloud.

chapters.title: The Recording That Wouldn't End
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Arriving in Kessho, Lena records an old woman's lullaby; on playback, a second voice hums beneath it, and the woman refuses to sing again, ever. Emotional beat: unease disguised as professional curiosity.

chapters.title: Twenty Years of Explanations
chapters.summary: Lena's POV, with flashbacks. He catalogs the house's noises — settling beams, wind, pipes — as he did as a child, but notices the kitchen table has five chairs though the family was four. Beat: the comfort of rationalization beginning to crack.

chapters.title: The Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Reviewing photos from his first week, he finds an added chair in every shot, positioned slightly nearer the head of the table than the day before. His grandmother's portrait seems to watch him. Beat: dread becomes undeniable.

chapters.title: Letters Nobody Wrote
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Lena and his sister Mika. Mika arrives unannounced, holding a letter in their grandmother's handwriting asking her to come home — though grandma died two years ago. Beat: the family is being summoned.

chapters.title: Auntie Sato's Papers
chapters.summary: Sato's POV. The village's last original resident reviews sale documents from the Kirisawa Development Group, hesitating over a clause requiring 'full transfer of all residents.' She remembers what happened to the Hara family in 1968. Beat: history surfacing.

chapters.title: What the Village Won't Sing Twice
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. At the community hall, elders perform festival songs; one man begins a verse about 'the guest at the table' and is silenced mid-line by the others. Lena archives the fragment anyway. Beat: loyalty enforced through silence.

chapters.title: Brother, Come Down
chapters.summary: Mika's POV. Their brother Theo arrives, hostile and broke, claiming he got a job offer dated from the house's address. That night all three hear a chair scrape upstairs in the sealed room. Beat: the family reassembles under false pretenses.

chapters.title: The Sealed Room
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. He opens the room his grandfather locked, finding a fourth place setting preserved under dust, a 1968 newspaper about a vanished surveyor, and his grandfather's unfinished letter of confession. Beat: guilt inherited, literally.

chapters.title: Counting Days
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs via Lena's field recordings. The chair in new photographs now sits at the table's head. Mika starts sleepwalking toward the kitchen; Theo finds mud on his shoes every morning despite drought. Beat: escalation, loss of control.

chapters.title: Kirisawa's Representative
chapters.summary: Third-person limited on Ms. Ayame Kirisawa. Polished and patient, she visits Sato daily, and Lena notices she never casts a shadow in the hallway mirror. She knows exactly what the clause means. Beat: the antagonist revealed as something older than the company.

chapters.title: The Hara House
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. He explores the abandoned Hara property and finds the same extra-chair phenomenon frozen in old photographs — six chairs for a family of five, then an empty house. Beat: pattern recognized; this has happened before and will happen again.

chapters.title: Grandfather's Confession
chapters.summary: Lena's POV, reading the letter. In 1968 his grandfather took payment to falsify the surveyor's death as accident, binding the family to the thing beneath Kessho as 'resident witnesses.' The song is a leash. Beat: the theme of loyalty vs. truth made explicit.

chapters.title: Mika Sings
chapters.summary: Mika's POV. Sleepwalking, Mika sings the forbidden verse perfectly in a voice not her own, then wakes with no memory and blood under her fingernails. Lena realizes the entity can wear them. Beat: terror turns intimate.

chapters.title: Theo Signs Nothing
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Kirisawa offers Theo money to sign as 'current resident,' promising the rest of the family immunity. Tempted, he nearly does — until he sees his own reflection already seated at the table in a window's reflection. Beat: betrayal narrowly averted.

chapters.title: The Village Turns
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. When Lena shows the elders the evidence, they exile him instead, insisting the arrangement protects everyone. Sato secretly gives him her copy of the deed and the true count: signatures required, days remaining. Beat: isolation; allies are scarce.

chapters.title: Fourteen Chairs
chapters.summary: Mika's POV. Every photo in the house now shows fourteen chairs. The kitchen fills nightly with the sound of a dinner party no one hosts. Grandma's voice thanks them for coming home. Beat: the haunting reaches full manifestation.

chapters.title: Ayame's Terms
chapters.summary: Kirisawa's POV. She reveals the entity's bargain honestly: a resident must sign willingly, or it takes residents unwillingly, starting with children. She believes feeding it is mercy. Beat: antagonist's logic laid bare, horrifyingly reasonable.

chapters.title: The Last Resident
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Sato dies peacefully in her sleep, making Lena — by blood and by deed — the last resident. That night the chair stands empty at the head of the table, waiting for a signature. Beat: point of no return.

chapters.title: The Song Sung Whole
chapters.summary: Climax, Lena's POV. In the village square, Lena performs the entire forbidden song, naming his grandfather's crime publicly, breaking the silence that sustained the lie. The house screams; the chairs rearrange; the ground opens beneath the threshold. Beat: truth as weapon.

chapters.title: Signature
chapters.summary: Climax continued, Lena's POV. At the table, facing the thing wearing his grandmother's smile, Lena signs the deed — but writes a new clause aloud, offering remembrance instead of servitude: the family will keep its story sung, annually, truthfully. The entity considers. Beat: negotiation with the unknowable.

chapters.title: Empty Chairs
chapters.summary: Resolution, alternating family POVs. The house stands vacant; the photographs show only four chairs, worn and honest. Mika, Theo, and Lena leave Kessho together, changed and estranged-but-bound. Beat: survival without restoration.

chapters.title: Recorded, Not Forgotten
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Lena's POV, one year later. At a folk archive, Lena plays the corrected recording — the whole song, both voices, named and credited. A listener asks about the humming underneath. Lena says: 'That's the part we owe.' Final image: a single chair, kept deliberately empty at his own table. Beat: belonging redefined as responsibility.
